Complete Empirical Research Plan

1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Random-effects meta-regression (a “meta-analysis of natural experiments”).  
Rationale:  
• The raw material is a collection of 31 already-credible causal estimates, each generated with its own quasi-experimental design (DID, IV, RDD, etc.).  
• The research question asks for the average marginal effect across U.S. contexts and for systematic effect heterogeneity.  
• A random-effects framework treats each study as one draw from an underlying distribution of true causal effects and allows moderator variables (spending type, baseline funding, poverty, urbanicity, etc.) to explain between-study variance.  
• The strategy is appropriate when (i) the internal validity of each study is high, but (ii) external validity is uncertain and must be modeled statistically.

2. Treatment and Control  
Treatment variable: A $1,000 (2018 dollars) increase in annual per-pupil spending sustained for four consecutive years. Every study estimate has already been rescaled to this common treatment.  
Control group: A hypothetical “no‐increase” group implied by each study’s identification design. Because we only observe study-level treatment effects, the counterfactual is embedded in each author’s research design; for the meta-analysis it is simply the absence of the $1,000 × 4-year spending shock.  
Timing / Event: Varies by study and is already incorporated. The meta-dataset records the average treatment window length (4 years) and follow-up horizon for each outcome.  
Running variable & cutoff: Not applicable (meta-analysis, not a single RDD).

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
A1. Unbiasedness of primary estimates – Each included study provides an internally valid causal estimate of the standardized treatment.  
Plausibility: High; the sample comprises peer-reviewed or working-paper designs judged as quasi-experimental.  
A2. Independence (or correctly modeled dependence) – True effects across studies are independent draws, or any within-study correlation is modeled.  
Plausibility: Moderate; some studies supply multiple outcomes that are correlated. We will cluster by study ID or use multilevel models.  
A3. No systematic publication/selective-reporting bias – The distribution of published effects is not truncated in a way that correlates with study precision.  
Plausibility: Questionable; we will test and adjust for funnel-plot asymmetry.  
A4. Correct scaling – All estimates are accurately converted to “per $1,000 per-pupil for four years” in SD units.  
Plausibility: Reasonable; conversions can be audited.  
A5. Effect heterogeneity captured by moderators – Observable study-level moderators explain heterogeneity; any remaining heterogeneity is random.  
Plausibility: Imperfect but standard in random-effects work; we will report τ² (between-study variance) and prediction intervals.

4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation  
T1. Publication / file-drawer bias.  
Fix: Funnel plots, Egger regression, trim-and-fill, and selection-model sensitivity analysis (e.g., p-curve).  
T2. Correlated measurement error and moderator values (e.g., low-quality studies from certain regions).  
Fix: Include study-quality indicators and region fixed effects; perform leave-one-out and leave-cluster-out robustness checks.  
T3. Multiple dependent estimates from the same study (violates independence).  
Fix: Use multilevel (study × outcome) meta-regression with random intercepts for study ID, or cluster-robust variance estimators (CRVE).

5. R Code Outline
```r
# 0. Packages ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(metafor)   # meta-regression
library(clubSandwich) # CRVE for meta
library(fixest)    # robustness check alternative

# 1. Data Load --------------------------------------------------------------
meta <- read_csv("school_spending_meta.csv")  # assume wide format

# 2. Variable Construction --------------------------------------------------
meta <- meta %>%
  mutate(
    yi   = effect_estimate,   # standardized effect (SDs)
    sei  = effect_se,         # standard error
    vi   = sei^2,             # variance
    capital = if_else(spending_type=="capital",1,0),
    low_income = if_else(poverty_rate > .5, 1, 0),
    high_baseline = if_else(baseline_spend > median(baseline_spend, na.rm=TRUE),1,0),
    rural = if_else(urbanicity=="rural",1,0)
  )

# 3. Main Random-Effects Meta-Regression ------------------------------------
# Multi-level random intercept for study_id (in case of multiple rows per study)
m1 <- rma.mv(yi, vi,
             mods = ~ capital + low_income + high_baseline + rural,
             random = ~ 1 | study_id,
             data = meta,
             method = "REML")
summary(m1)

# 4. Funnel Plot and Egger Test (Publication Bias) --------------------------
funnel(m1)
regtest(m1, model="lm")  # Egger

# 5. Robust CRVE Standard Errors -------------------------------------------
m1_crve <- coef_test(m1, vcov="CR2")  # cluster-robust

# 6. Leave-One-Study-Out Robustness ----------------------------------------
loo <- leave1out(m1)
plot(loo)

# 7. Prediction for New Context (e.g., poor, low baseline) ------------------
newdata <- data.frame(capital=0, low_income=1, high_baseline=0, rural=0)
predict(m1, newmods=as.matrix(newdata))
```

6. Expected Results  
Direction: Positive—the literature generally finds that more money improves test scores and attainment.  
Magnitude (prior): Roughly +0.04 standard deviations in test scores and +1.5 percentage-points in high-school graduation per $1,000 per-pupil for four years, with larger gains (≈ +0.07 SD) in low-income contexts and near-zero effects for capital spending in already high-spend districts.

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1 = satisfied, 0 = questionable)  
C1: Comprehensive literature search …………………… 1  
C2: Internal validity of included studies ………………… 1  
C3: Independence / correct clustering of estimates …… 0.5 (some dependence)  
C4: Absence of publication bias ………………………… 0 (uncertain)  
C5: Correct scaling & harmonization of treatment …… 1  
Total ≈ 3.5 / 5 – Reasonably credible but results should be interpreted with caution due to residual publication bias and dependence concerns.
